I have never taken a bulb from the plant because it's a cardinal sin among wild vegetable enthusiasts. Oy the leaves.

Supplies: A razor blade cutter, shopping bag, gloves, hiking gear and willing to scrounge about

Target:

Tender leaves that are about as long as your hand span. Small leaves don't have as much flavor. So go for something longer than your index finger.

Do not target blooming plants. Flower is purplish in color. The leaves are tough and you missed the season.

Harvest method:

The bulb has a red spot towards the top so cut the stalk just above that. This means next year the bulb will bloom again.

Both the stalk and leaves are edible like spinach so you're good to go.

Basic prep:

Dump your score into a bucket or basin of water and wash generously. Get the fox piss off and other dirt and bugs.

There is a slight skin like an onion has that's really thin and you need to get it off. I usey index middle and thumb finger nails to to bull it towards the cut. This can be done before or after boiling but I think before is better since boiling gets the little pieces left off rather than have to rinse again after boiling.

Boiling:

This depends on how you eat it. If you go BBQ style don't boil. Other reciepe I would. Boiling should be thought of as a disinfectant rather than a prep stage. So flash boil for a few seconds. In and out quick so you don't destroy the cell strength. If you do falah boil you can later freeze extra leaves in small bundles. I normally went with a 2 person serving size of spaghetti noodles.

Recipe BBQ style:

Well, technically not a BBQ but open flame is used so BBQ. It's a Korean BBQ style were you grill the meat on a skillet or the flat part grill. You could do this with a steak in the kitchen easily. Right about when the meat is cooked add handfullls of the wonder leaves and let them break down like cabbage. But don't go as far as canned spinache. The leaves are like onions then.

Another favorite is adding them to ramen. Fuck yeah!! Kick ass! I bet they would work in minestrone or tomato soup! Don't over boil the leaves!

Last but more Japanese would be creating a sweet miso paste sauce like dressing. The sauce is miso paste, mirin, sugar and rice vinegar. You can't skip the miso paste but you can get away with balancing just white vinegar and sugar. You want to stay on the salty side with a taint of sweet and vinegar. Boil the leaves to so they are limp and you have just broken the cell structure. Rinse and cool to room or even fridge temperature. The dressing doesnt need to be boiled but the sugar should be dissolved. You can either mix the dressing up with the leaves and clump out in a side dish or keep them in bunches and slice horizontally in inch groups and pour the dressing over heartily.

The miso method is my favorite!

I think you can pull a 1700 for now, and the AM4 platform should be around for a while. It's not guaranteed but we should see 7nm CPUs on AM4. So the motherboard will last, Intel loves to jump sockets and if you need a new Intel CPU, you'll need a new motherboard too, which will add to the cost of an Intel system. I went with 16GB of RAM, so you don't have to worry about running out of RAM in the future and it should last you several years. An 8 core Ryzen should last you a good three or five years before it becomes a problem.

The 480 has aged somewhat well but it would probably be the weakest link in this build. But I am expecting some longevity out of AM4, so the CPU and motherboard should last you at least a few years. I would imagine in two years or so you'd want to get a new graphics card and keep the rest of your system the same (provided you mind the PSU, you may want to upgrade it to higher wattage).

I'm assuming you aren't the type to upgrade very often. If you are, an Intel quad for less money on the CPU and more on a graphics card will work better in the short term, but you'll be stranded on a socket that will probably be dead in a year and you won't have any upgrade paths beyond a quad core.

If you can wait for the 6 core Ryzens, you can take about $100 out of the CPU and get a better graphics card. Oddly enough, I went to check on what graphics card would fit into the $300 to $350 price range and there's not anything good. You have 28nm GPUs (which are bad, the new ones are 14nm), GTX 1070 around $400, 480 at $200, and 1060 at $250. I assume we'll see a GTX 1060 Ti or something from AMD that fits in that price bracket soon.

But I think it is best for you to wait a little bit. I have been watching people say Intel's lower core count is enough for a long time, and those people always get bitten by it.
